name: Cost Simulation
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Running the Numbers a Thousand Times
lesson.summary: Cost simulation runs a cost projection model repeatedly under randomized, varying assumptions, such as fluctuating gas prices or bursts of congestion, to produce a distribution of likely total costs rather than a single forecast or a handful of hand-picked scenarios.
lesson.body:
The cost projection model covered in the previous section produces a small number of hand-picked scenarios: low, expected, high. Cost simulation goes a step further by treating the uncertain inputs to that model, transaction volume, gas price, token valuation, congestion frequency, as random variables with a plausible range of behavior, then running the model many times with randomly drawn values for each input. The result is not one number or three numbers, but a distribution: a picture of how likely different total cost outcomes actually are, which is closer to how blockchain costs actually behave in the real world than any single forecast can be.

This matters because blockchain costs are driven by inputs that do not move smoothly. Gas prices on a congested public network can spike well above their typical range during a short burst of demand, such as a popular NFT mint or a period of high market volatility, and then fall back down once demand subsides. A model that only looks at average or typical gas prices will systematically understate the cost of operating during exactly those spikes, and for a system that depends on submitting time-sensitive transactions, like a lending protocol that needs to liquidate a position before it becomes undercollateralized, the cost of operating during a spike, not the average cost, is often the number that actually matters for planning.

The technique borrowed here is the same one used broadly in financial risk modeling: repeatedly sample from a probability distribution for each uncertain input, run the full cost model on each sampled combination, and collect the resulting total costs across all the runs. Doing this many times over produces an approximate probability distribution of total cost outcomes, from which a planner can read off, for example, the cost level that will not be exceeded in a stated share of simulated scenarios, giving a concrete sense of downside risk rather than just a best guess.

Cost simulation is only as good as the assumptions baked into the distributions it samples from. If historical gas price volatility understates how bad future congestion could get, because a new application category drives unprecedented demand, or because a network upgrade changes the fee mechanism entirely, the simulation will confidently produce a distribution that no longer reflects reality. Simulation manages known uncertainty well; it does not protect against being wrong about what the uncertain inputs even are, which is why the scenario assumptions from the underlying projection model still need periodic review rather than being trusted indefinitely.

A cost simulation, however sophisticated, only ever describes half of the decision: what the system will cost. The next section pairs that cost picture with an estimate of the benefits a blockchain system is expected to deliver, so the two can be weighed against each other directly.
